REASONING:
Step 1 – Frame the project  
- Objective: improve efficiency of delivery and access to selected administrative services in Albania.  
- Scope: three components – (1) backend systems (IT upgrades, business‑process re‑engineering), (2) citizen interface (one‑stop‑shop centre, online services, feedback mechanisms), (3) capacity building (performance management, training, communications).  
- Delivery model: IBRD loan US$32 m (PPF US$2 m, Results‑Based Financing US$25 m, Technical Assistance US$5 m) with a results‑based disbursement linked to five DLIs.  
- Timeline: implementation 26‑Aug‑2015 to 30‑Sep‑2020; effectiveness 31‑Dec‑2020.  
- Budget: total project cost US$74.1 m, Bank financing US$32 m.  
- Key stakeholders: Ministry of Finance (borrower), Ministry of State for Innovation & Public Administration (responsible agency), ADISA (implementing agency/PMU), NAIS, Prime Minister’s Delivery Unit, Inter‑ministerial Public Services Committee, multiple service agencies (IPRO, SII, etc.).  
- External dependencies: EU assistance, e‑Albania portal, ICT infrastructure, private‑sector partners for possible PPPs, legislative approval of reform policy.

Step 2 – Category sweep (candidate risks with supporting text)  
Technical  
1. “Seven institutions … have no IT system in place… new IT systems will be built in phases.”  
2. “NAIS is working to connect existing online registries to the government gateway… 21 institutions are connected, 11 more to be connected in 2015.”  

Financial  
3. “The overall financial management risk is rated as Substantial.”  
4. “Procurement risk rating is High.”  
5. “No disbursements under RBF will be made until DLI#5 is achieved.”  

Schedule  
6. “The compressed implementation timeline is a potential risk, which is mitigated by the project’s span and incentives to deliver up to 2020.”  
7. “The central CSC building in Tirana … core features and size have not yet been decided. Various models for financing, construction and management, including PPPs, are currently being considered.”  
8. “Regulatory reforms … will be implemented through omnibus legislation, expected to be passed by the end of 2016.”  

Stakeholder  
9. “Bureaucratic resistance could stifle efforts to improve back‑office functions.”  
10. “Only 60 internet users per 100 people in 2013, indicating low internet penetration.”  

Political/Regulatory  
11. “The Reform Policy Document must be approved by the Strategic Planning Committee chaired by the Prime Minister; DLI#5 requires this.”  

Environmental  
12. “Potential environmental impacts … include dust and noise, waste generation, material supply, use of machinery, possible traffic and safety issues.”  

Social  
13. “Risk that the focus on state‑of‑the‑art means … could diminish access of the poor and vulnerable because of diversion of attention and resources.”  

Organizational  
14. “Very weak procurement capacity at ADISA as a newly created agency.”  
15. “Insufficient institutional and implementation capacity of the Ministry of State for Innovation … implications for project implementation and longer‑term sustainability.”  

Step 3 – Evidence filter  
All 15 candidates are directly quoted in the appraisal document; none are discarded.

Step 4 – Assess & mitigate  
| ID | Likelihood (1‑5) | Impact (1‑5) | Justification | Mitigation |
|----|------------------|--------------|---------------|------------|
| R01 | 4 | 4 | New IT systems for seven agencies with no legacy platform risk delays. | Conduct detailed IT needs assessment, phased rollout, dedicated technical team, and regular milestone reviews. |
| R02 | 3 | 4 | Interoperability of 21+ agencies to the gateway may encounter technical mismatches. | Define clear data‑exchange standards, pilot integrations, allocate resources for NAIS coordination, and schedule extensive testing. |
| R03 | 3 | 4 | Substantial financial‑management risk indicates possible mis‑allocation of funds. | Provide intensive FM training, hire experienced finance specialists, implement robust internal controls and quarterly audits. |
| R04 | 3 | 3 | High procurement risk can cause cost overruns and delays. | Strengthen procurement unit, adopt World Bank procurement guidelines, engage experienced procurement specialists, and use Bank technical assistance. |
| R05 | 3 | 4 | RBF cash‑flow depends on DLI#5 (strategic plan approval); delay blocks disbursements. | Develop detailed work‑plan for strategic‑plan approval, monitor progress, provide TA to expedite DLI#5, keep contingency cash reserves. |
| R06 | 4 | 3 | Compressed timeline may lead to missed milestones. | Implement rigorous schedule monitoring, critical‑path analysis, buffer periods, and weekly steering‑committee reviews. |
| R07 | 3 | 4 | Uncertainty over CSC design, financing and construction could postpone opening. | Finalise design early, secure financing (including PPP if needed), fast‑track permits, appoint experienced construction manager, monitor progress. |
| R08 | 3 | 3 | Delay in omnibus legislation stalls regulatory reforms and BPR. | Accelerate drafting, engage legal experts, coordinate with IPSC to prioritize bill, set firm deadline for parliamentary passage. |
| R09 | 3 | 3 | Bureaucratic resistance may impede front‑office reforms. | Conduct change‑management workshops, involve senior officials early, communicate benefits, create incentives for cooperation. |
| R10 | 4 | 3 | Low internet penetration limits uptake of e‑services, threatening project outcomes. | Deploy assisted‑digital access points, mobile kiosks, training for low‑skill users, maintain strong non‑digital channels, run outreach campaigns. |
| R11 | 3 | 4 | Political delay in approving Reform Policy Document blocks DLI#5 and RBF payments. | Provide high‑level political liaison, align reform timeline with government calendar, secure PM endorsement, monitor approval process closely. |
| R12 | 2 | 2 | Construction may cause dust, noise, waste, traffic, but EMP is planned. | Implement EMP measures: dust suppression, noise barriers, waste‑management plan, traffic control, and monitor compliance. |
| R13 | 3 | 3 | Emphasis on high‑end digital services could marginalise poor/vulnerable groups. | Preserve existing service points, expand assisted access, targeted outreach, monitor access indicators for disadvantaged groups. |
| R14 | 3 | 3 | Very weak procurement capacity at ADISA risks ineffective procurement. | Recruit experienced procurement staff, provide procurement training, use Bank assistance for document review, adopt transparent procedures. |
| R15 | 3 | 3 | Insufficient capacity of the Ministry of Innovation threatens implementation and sustainability. | Strengthen ministry staff via capacity‑building TA, hire additional experts, define clear responsibilities, establish performance metrics. |

Step 5 – Consolidate  
All identified risks are retained (15 items); duplicates merged where appropriate.
